%%
%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
\mj{Online moral discussions often converge on a prevailing judgment, but agreement alone reveals little about how dissent is received or what reasoning develops around it. We examine minority participation in Reddit’s r/AmItheAsshole through comment reception, moral reasons articulated in comment–reply exchanges, and readers’ responses to dissent. In high-agreement discussions, minority judgments receive lower scores but attract approximately 4.9 times as many replies and 6.1 times the reply depth of majority judgments. Blaming dissent against a defending majority attracts more engagement than defending dissent against a blaming majority. Replies to minority judgments predominantly challenge them, whereas replies to majority judgments predominantly offer support. Yet rejection can coexist with additional reasoning: Replies to defending dissent more often introduce moral reasons absent from their parent comments than replies to majority judgments (69.1\% vs. 48.2\%) A randomized reader experiment with 80 readers compares two majority threads (Highly Scored) with one majority and one minority thread (Balanced). Readers in Balanced report greater consideration of why someone might reach a different judgment and lower mean judgment certainty, while observed majority-alignment proportions are similar across conditions. Together, these findings suggest that the role of dissent extends beyond whether its judgment gains approval, encompassing the reasons articulated in response and the alternatives readers consider.}
\end{abstract}
